source: trans. Lee M. Hollander, Old Norse Poems (1936)

1.1:
Hialti: “Awake, arise, rally, friends!
All ye foremost athelings of Hrólf!
Awake not to wine nor to your wives’ converse,
but rather to Gondul’s game of war.”

2.1:
Biarki: (drowsily responds, calling out to a thrall:)
“Bring a fardel of fagots to kindle the fire!
Brush thou the hearth and blow in the embers!
Let the kindling crackle to kindle the logs:
’tis winsome, with warm hand to welcome friends.”

5.1:
“Hold firm your hilts, ye chosen housecarls,
shield flung on shoulder, to show ye are men;
breast open ’gainst breast offer we to our foemen:
beak against beak, so shall battle the eagles.

6.1:
“Foremost among fighters bold Hiorvarth fares,
glorying in swordplay, in gold-helm dight;
after him are marching martial hosts of Gauts,
with ring-laid helms and rattling spears.

7.1:
“Skuld him egged on, the Skioldung queen,
to his kin to be false, his king to betray;
raving she is and bereft of reason,
by evil norns for ill created.”

8.1:
“Now their last cup for kingsmen is poured,
after his liege-lord shall no one live
but he show him fearful and shrink from blows,
or be too listless his lord to avenge.

10.1:
“Lift thou now, Hrút, thy light-haired brow,
leave thy bower, for battle is nigh.
10.2: the towers are tumbling, the castle-gates tremble.”

11.1:
Hialti: “Bidest thou yet, Biarki? Do sleep-runes bind thee?
Come forth now with me ere thee fire assail!
We fend off our foes as we do bears—with firebrands:
the castle crumbles, the king’s hall flames.”

12.1:
Hialti: “Let us rally our ranks as Hrólf us taught,
the hero who hewed down the ring-hoarder.
Wretched was Hrœrek though he riches owned:
but gold he gathered, not gallant men.

13.1:
“Hrólf harried on Hrœrek. He ransom offered—
before the gates disgorged his purse its gold:
he strewed before stronghold stores of treasure.
Then was lavished on foe what on friends was saved.

14.1:
“Though our liege him slew: he allotted the hoard
among faithful followers, refused it himself.
Nothing him gladdened but he gave it to them:
to award it to warriors naught was too welcome.

15.1:
“The most large-hearted lord lifeless has sunk;
lost is the life men will longest remember:
he ran to the sword-play as river toward sea,
fared against foe like the fleet-footed stag.

16.1:
“A burn of blood from the battle-field flows,
as Hiorvarth arnong hosts Hild’s-play speedeth.
But the sword-giver smiles in his sleep of death,
as at bountiful banquet he beakers emptied.

17.1:
“Fróthi’s kinsman on the Fýri Plains
his gold rings sowed, glad in his mind;
him we joyfully follow on his journey to Hel,
manly of speech and firm of mettle.

18.1:
“Blows of our brands shall back our faith,
the glory of great deeds never is forgotten.
Latched and locked the hall still is right.
A third time, Biarki, I bid thee come forth!”

20.1:
“On an isle was I born, barren and little;
twelve demesnes gave me Hrólf to master,
realms to rule, and ruddy gold, too—
his sister to wife; here’s worth to requite.
 (He plunges into battle:)

21.1:
“Shields on your shoulders, if ye shun not death!
Only the craven covers him now.
Bare your breasts! Your bucklers fling down!
Gold-weighted arm the glaive best wields.

22.1:
“With my steel erst I struck the ‘wild stag’ in battle,
with my short-sword slew him which Snirtir is named.
Hero’s name got I when its hilt I gripped—
when Agnar Ingialdsson’s life I ended.

23.1:
“ ’Gainst my head he hewed, but Hœking broke,
on Biarki’s brow his blade was shattered.
Then raised I Snirtir, through his ribs thrust him,
his right hand and right leg I lopped with one blow.

24.1:
“Never was there, I ween, a more warlike hero
than when, sword-hewn, sank the son of Ingiald:
lifeless he lay and laughed toward death;
to Valholl’s gates he gleefully hied him.

25.1:
“To his heart I hewed the hero but now,
young in years but unyielding in spirit;
through his buckler I battered, naught booted him his hauberk:
my Snirtir but seldom slackens its blow.

26.1:
“Guard you now, ye gallant Gautish chieftains!
Athelings only enter this battle!

27.1:
“His loved son now loses many a lord;
but for barons, not bondmen Hel’s bars will be lowered.
More closely comes the clash of battle,
three blows I get for one I give.

28.1:
“Alone in the strife I stand amongst the slain.
A bulwark I build me of fallen bodies.
Where is now he who whetted me before,
and tempted me sore, as though twelve lives he had?”

29.1:
Hialti: “Few are the followers, but far I am not.
strong is now need of stout-hearted men;
battered is my buckler, broken and shattered—
yourself may see it: sight goes before hearsay.
Doest battle now, Biarki, as thou bidedst before?”

30.1:
Biarki: “Thy spiteful speech spurs me no longer:
not I am the cause that tardy I came.
Now a Swedish sword sorely has struck me;
through my war-weeds it went as though water it cleft.”

31.1:
“But where is Óthin, the one-eyed grey-beard?
Say now, Hrút, swiftly: Seest thou him nowhere?”

32.1:
Hrút: “Lower thy eye and look through my arm,
sign then thy view with victory-runes:
unscathed shalt thou, Biarki, then scan with thy glance
and fasten thy eyes on the father of victory.”

33.1:
Biarki: “Could I fasten my eyes on Frigg’s husband now,
the swift shield-swinger and Sleipnir’s rider,
his life would lose the war-god at Leire—
blood for blood then would Biarki crave.

34.1:
“Here by my chieftain’s head I shall sink now,
thou by his feet shalt find thee a rest.
Booty-seekers on battle field shall bear me out:
the great-souled king’s gifts even the dead forget not.

35.1:
“Soon greedy eagles will gorge on our bodies,
ramping ravens will rend our limbs.
to high-minded, hardy hero it is seeming
dying to dwell by his king rich in deeds.”

1.1:
“Go from the grey-beard! No longer make game of me,
ye deedless swains in the Danish court!
No outcast is the old man before you:
oft hoary hair hideth a hardy mind.

2.1:
“I formerly followed Fróthi for years,
sate in the high-seat, and was served before others;
but now I sit nameless and unknown in the hall,
I like a fish at ebb-tide finding a waterhole.

3.1:
“I formerly sate on soft cushions;
now in a corner I sit, crowded by every one.
Fain out of doors would they drive the grey-beard
but wall and wainscot gave welcome foothold.

4.1:
“The courtiers laugh at me who come from afar off,
no one gets up to greet me or to cheer the guest!
What be the ways now in the hall of the Skioldungs?
I should like to learn Leire’s new breeding.

5.1:
“Thinkest thou, Ingiald, as at ease thou sittest,
to avenge Fróthi, thy father, on his banesmen?
Or are you pleased, rather to fill your paunch
than to make stern war on the murderers of your father?

6.1:
“That feared I, when farewell to the folkwarder I said,
that slain by the sword he soon would lie.
From Fróthi afar the folklands I roamed
when I learned that our liege had been laid low by Saxons.

7.1:
“Had that time I been with the thane’s shield-bearers,
then not deedless had I seen my dear lord’s fall:
my sword had then smitten the Saxon traitors,
or else had I fallen by Fróthi’s side.

8.1:
“Now on wilding ways I wended from Sweden,
hoping to find Fróthi’s heir-taker—
and find a feaster but for food hankering,
and instead of a king, a coward and wanton.

9.1:
“But sooth did say the Swedish king—
that ‘deedless scions follow doughty father.’
Shall strangers steal the stores of your father?
Shall his red-gold rings fall in robbers’ hands?”

10.1:
“Away from the warrior with your woman’s finery!
About your own brow bind your fillet,
or else your husband’s, who will highly prize it,
fingering for food steaked fowls’ inwards.

11.1:
“Evil art, thou, Ingiald’s mistress!
Saxland’s ways soft to Sealand thou broughtest!
In the king’s kitchen cook they now tidbits,
such as war-workers ne’er would have eaten.

12.1:
“But on board, bloody, the meat of beeves
was laid for strong men as they right the battlefield.
In their frosted beards oft bit the rowers,
nor slaked their thirst with sweet milk for babies.

13.1:
“Athelings eleven, all told, were there
with Haki, when we rode the horse-of-the-sea.
Beigath and Belgi at board with us sate;
seldom on sea fared swains more hardy.

14.1:
“With smoked salt meat we sated our hunger,
and slaked our thirst with swallows of ale;
nor was honeyed mead ever Haki’s delight,
nor soft bread, either, when at sea he fared.

15.1:
“But weregild no one e’er would have taken,
or by payment of pence in his purse borne his father;
nor was ever heard that the heir of his father
sate at festive board with his father’s banesmen.

16.1:
“So, when in the hall great heroes are spoken of,
and skalds are chanting the champions’ great deeds,
then in shame I hide under hood my glances,
for Fróthi’s first-born showed but faint-heartedness.

17.1:
“Why so sternly, Ingiald, starest thou at me?
Never saw the sneering Saxons such glances!
Thou who never didst win other warfare
than cutting down bread and killing puddings.

18.1:
“A cruel fate has befallen Fróthi’s kinsmen
when the king was given such a coward as heir:
no greater worth hast thou than a hunted goat,
or than sheep in shambles shrinking in terror.

19.1:
“Shall Sverting’s seed hold sway over Denmark,
Seated at Leire with Saxon warriors,
on thy lap whilst thou fondlest the linen-clad woman,
the fair-haired daughter of thy father’s banesman.

20.1:
“Rail now, Ingiald! Thou art awakened!
No more wavering weakness, thou warriors’ leader,
but slay with the sword all of Sverting’s kinsmen!
Alike be their death as alike was their deed!

21.1:
“Let thralls drag then the dead from the high-seat,
cart away the killed ones from the king’s mead-hall,
toss the dead out-of-doors— nor dig graves for them—
to feed on the heath foxes and ravens.

22.1:
“Still further shalt, Ingiald, if foresight thou hast,
put away the woman wily and evil!
The she-wolf’s whelps will take after her:
beware of the wolf though weak he be now.

23.1:
“Behold now, Hrauthi, thou who whettest to strife,
that full vengeance for Fróthi is taken:
the seven sons of Sverting by sword are laid low,
his false friends now are felled by Ingiald.

24.1:
“Though hoary my hair that hope never left me
that Fróthi’s first-born would not flinch in trial;
as only heir shall Ingiald rule here
over the lands of the Danes and Leire’s high-seat.”

1.1:
“A boy was I when they burned in hall,
with my father, the warrior host—
not far outside the firth of Thruma.

2.1:
“Was Harold of Agthir’s host overthrown—
had his kinsmen bewrayed the ring-breaker,
Fiori and Fýri, earl Freki’s heirs.
Were they Unni’s brothers, my own mother’s;

3.1:
“the time Herthióf Harold betrayed,
betrayed the king who trusted in him.
He robbed of his life the liege of Agthir,
and fetters fastened for his twain sons.

4.1:
“Me three winters old thence did bring
Hrosshársgrani to Horthaland;
at Ask gan I grow and strengthen,
saw none of my sib for nine summers.

5.1:
“Strength gat I mighty, grew stalwart my arms,
and long my legs, loathly my head;
as a gaby, dozing I gaping sate,
listless and lazy, on lower bench.

6.1:
“Then Víkar wended, from watch-fire faring,
Herthióf’s hostage, into the hall.
He knew me again by name and bade me
up to arise and answer him.

7.1:
“With hands and fingers he fathomed me:
were all my arms (much etin-like,)
to the wrists downward (rough and hairy,)
and my face bearded from brow to chin.

8.1:
“Then Harold’s heir the host gathered:
Sorkvir and Grettir and Hildigrím,
Erp and Ulf, Án and Skúma,
Hrói and Hrotti, which were Herbrand’s sons,

9.1:
“Stýr and Steinthór from Stath in the North,
gathered also old Gunnólf blesi.
Were then of us thirteen together:
a hardier host will hardly be found.

10.1:
“To Herthióf’s hall we hied us then,
shook its door-posts, broke down its gates,
shattered its bars, brandished our swords
where stood seventy stalwart warriors.

11.1:
“We vied with each other, Víkar to follow
since first and foremost in the flock he stood;
we hewed helmets and the heads that bore them,
sundered byrnies and broke through shields.

12.1:
“Was great glory granted to Víkar,
but Herthióf paid for his hateful deed:
some we wounded, and slew others;
not far was I stead when fell the king.

13.1:
“On the Vænir wert not with Víkar then,
east in the land at early morn,
in the field when we fought with Sísar:
were those doughty deeds of undying fame.

14.1:
“With his sword did he sorely wound me—
sharp-edged was it— through my shield cleaving.
My helm he hewed from off my head,
my chin he cleft clean to the jawteeth.

15.1:
“And on one side with his sword he cut me—
mightier than I— the midriff above;
but through the other he thrust his spear,
the cold iron, within it stood.

16.1:
“With my sword, Sísar’s side I cut then
with bitter brand, his belly athwart.
So wrathfully I raised my sword
that all my strength I bestowed on it.

17.1:
“Much Welsh gold gave me Víkar—
the red-gold ring which on wrist I wear,
of three marks’ weight; I Thruma gave him.
I followed the king fifteen summers.

18.1:
“I followed the king whom foremost I knew:
my life did I like best then.
’T was ere we fared— did foul trolls drive us—
to Horthaland: this happened last.

19.1:
“The outcome this, that Thór gave me
a nithing’s name, unnumbered woes—
.  .  .  .  .  .  .  .
19.2: I was fated fell things to do.

20.1:
“In high tree was I to hallow Víkar,
to give to the gods Geirthiof’s slayer.
Through his heart I thrust the thane with my spear:
of all my works most woeful this!

21.1:
“On wilding ways I wandered thence,
by the Horthar hated, with heart rueful,
bereft of rings and robbed of honor,
leaderless, forlorn in mind.

22.1:
“Now have I sought the Swedish lands,
the Ynglings’ seat, Uppsala halls.
A speechless poet, the prince’s sons
did let me stay— as long I shall.

23.1:
“They set me here brash swains between,
who scornfully scoff at the aged skald;
gleefully girding, they make game of me,
and lewdly laugh at the liege’s poet.

24.1:
“They ween they see on my own self
the etin mark of eight arms,
the time Hlórrithi Hergrím’s slayer
reft of his arms in the outmost North.

25.1:
“The men laugh when looking at me—
at my loathly mug and long snout,
my wolf-grey hair and hanging arms,
my scurvy neck and wrinkled skin.”

1.1:
Sóti: “What ails thee, Hiálmar? Thy hue is pale.
Great wounds, I ween, do weary thee;
thy helmet is hewn, thy hauberk eke:
at an end is now, atheling, thy life!”

2.1:
Hiálmar: “Wounds have I sixteen, is slit my byrnie,
dim grows my sight, I see no longer:
to my heart did hew, venom-hardened,
Angantýr’s sword slashing sharply.

3.1:
“Shall fair ladies never learn that I,
from blows me shielding, backward turned me;
nor shall ever Ingibiorg taunt me,
in Sigtúna sitting, that from sword-blows I fled.

4.1:
“Unwilling nowise, from women’s converse,
from their sweet songs I with Soti fared,
hastened to join the host to eastward,
went the last time forth from friends so dear.

5.1:
“Led me the white-browed liege’s daughter
to the outmost end of Agnafit.
Is borne out thus that back I would not
wend from this war: so the wise maid said.

6.1:
“From Ingibiorg— came ill-hap swiftly—
I fared forth, then, on fated day:
a lasting sorrow to the lady, this,
since not e’er after each other we’ll see.

7.1:
“To have and to hold I had five manors;
on that land to live misliked me, though.
Now, robbed of life, I lie here, spent,
by the sword wounded, on Sáms-isle’s shore.

8.1:
“Take with thee, Soti— my wish it is—
my helm and hauberk to the hall of the king.
Will it wring the heart of the ruler’s daughter
when shattered she sees what shielded my breast.

9.1:
“The red-gold ring from my right arm draw,
to Ingibiorg bring it, in her bower sitting.
Will yearn for me the young maiden,
since not e’er after each other we’ll see.

10.1:
“I see sitting in Sigtúna hall
the women who warned me of wending thence.
Will not ever after ale nor warriors
Hiálmar gladden here in this life.

11.1:
“Quaff with the king the crowd of housecarls
their ale gladly in Uppsala;
doth the mead many men overcome,
but me overmaster here many wounds.

12.1:
“Flies from the South the famished raven,
flieth with him the fallow eagle;
on the flesh of the fallen I shall feed them no more:
on my body both will batten now.”

1.1:
The Shepherd: “Who by himself hath come hither on isle?
Go thou straightway, get thee shelter!”

2.1:
Hervor: “I care not go and get me shelter:
not any one know I of the island’s men.
Ere hence thou hiest, in haste tell me:
where are the howes for Hiorvarth named?”

3.1:
The Shepherd: “Ask not of such, if sage thou art,
friend-of-vikings: thou ’rt on ferly ways;
let us fare hence so fast as feet will carry!
Without now is it awful for men.”

4.1:
Hervor: “This trinket’s thine if thou tell me this:
’t were hard to hold back the heroes’-friend.”
4.2:
The Shepherd: “Thou canst not give such golden trinkets,
such fair-shining rings, that I fare with thee.

5.1:
“ ’Tis folly, in faith, to fare thither
for a man alone in this murky dark:
is fire abroad, the barrows open,
burn field and fen: let us flee in haste.”

6.1:
Hervor: “I scorn to dread a din like this,
though fires do burn all about the isle!
Let not men who are dead unman us, shepherd,
with fear so swiftly, but say thou on!”

7.1:
The Shepherd: “Is Hel’s gate lifted, the howes do ope,
the edge of the isle is all afire—
awful is it to be without:
to thy ships hie thee in haste, oh maiden!”

8.1:
Hervor: “Such nightly blaze ye cannot build
that of their fires afraid I grow:
will Hervor’s heart not be horror-struck,
e’en though a ghost in grave-door stood.

9.1:
“Awake, Angantýr! Wakes thee Hervor,
thy only bairn, born to Sváva;
the bitter brand from thy belt gird thou,
which swinking dwarfs for Sváfrlami wrought.

10.1:
“Hervarth, Hiorvarth, Hrani, Angantýr!
I awake you all, ye wights neath mold
with helmets and byrnies and bitter swords,
with gory spears and all gear of war.

11.1:
“Have Arngrím’s sons, the evil men’s,
their corpses become to clay and mold,
seeing that none of the sons of Eyfura
with me will speak in Munar Bay.

12.1:
“May all of you feel within your ribs
as though in ant-hill your ill bones rotted,
but the sword ye fetch me forged by Dvalin:
it befits not ghosts to guard prized arms.”

13.1:
Angantýr: “Hervor, daughter, why doest call me
with cold curses? They will cost thee dear!
Bereft of reason and raving art thou,
that with wildered thought thou wak’st the dead.

14.1:
“Neither father me buried nor fellow kinsmen:
(thy brothers’ banesmen this barrow raised.)
The twain who lived did Tyrfing win—
now one of the victors wields it at last.”

15.1:
Hervor: “Thou say’st not sooth! May so the gods
leave thee whole in howe as thou hast not
Tyrfing with thee: unwilling art
to give thy daughter her dearest wish,”

16.1:
Angantýr: “Hardly human I hold thee, maiden,
about barrows who hoverest at night,
with graven spear and Gothic iron,
with helmet and byrnie, the hall’s gate before,

17.1:
Hervor: “Howbeit, human was I held to be
ere hither I hied me, your hall to seek:
out of howe hand me the hater-of-byrnies,
the dwarfs’ handiwork: ’t will not do to hide it!”

18.1:
Angantýr: “Under my shoulders hidden lies Hiálmar’s bane,
about its blade blazes fire:
in this wide world know I no woman born
who would dare to wield the dreaded sword.”

19.1:
Hervor: “Would I hold in hand— if have it I might—
the bitter brand, and in battle wield it,
Not a whit fear I the fire blazing:
it swiftly sinks as I seek it with eye.”

20.1:
Angantýr: “I tell thee, Hervor— heed my warning!—
what will happen, thou heroes’ daughter!
I say but sooth: will this sword become
the slayer of all thy sib and kin.”

21.1:
Hervor: “Thus shall I deal with you dead men’s bones
that in your graves ye get no rest:
hand me, Angantýr, out of the howe
the sword wherewith thou slewest Hiálmar!”

22.1:
Angantýr: “Witless art thou, and of wanton mind,
like a fool to fling thee into fire blazing!
Out of howe, rather, shall I hand the sword,
hardy maiden, nor withhold it from thee.”

23.1:
Hervor: “Well then doest thou, warriors’-offspring,
out of the howe to hand Tyrfing
which liefer to me, thou lord-of-battle,
than now to have all Norroway.”

24.1:
Angantýr: “Thou little knowest, luckless woman,
what ill thou ’st wrought with reckless speech:
I say but sooth: will this sword become
the slayer of all thy sib and kin.”

25.1:
Hervor: “To my ships on shore now shall I hie me:
is the hero’s daughter happy in mind.
Little reck I, ruler of men,
whether my sons will slay each other.”

26.1:
Angantýr: “Thou ’lt have it through life and long joy in it;
but keep thou hidden Hiálmar’s-slayer,
nor touch its edges: on the twain is poison.
Is that bitter brand baneful to all.

27.1:
“Thou ’lt have a son who hereafter
will wield Tyrfing and trust his strength;
Heithrek will he be hight of men,
and mightiest grow of men under heaven.

28.1:
“Farewell, daughter! I would fain give thee
the thews of twelve men if thou ’ldst but heed me—
their lives and strength, the stored-up wealth
which Arngrím’s sons left after them.”

29.1:
Hervor: “Shall I hie me hence. Happily may ye—
I long to be gone— live in your howe.
But lately I lingered ’twixt life and death,
when all about me blazed the fires.”

2.1:
Was Hloth born there in Hunnish folk-lands—
with dagger and broadsword and byrnie long,
with ring-decked helmet and sharp-hewing sword,
with horses well-broken, in the hallowed land.

3.1:
Rode Hloth from the East, King Heithrek’s first-born,
to the halls where dwell the dauntless Goths—
to Árheimar— to claim his heir-lands.
There was Angantýr drinking arvel for Heithrek.

4.1:
Before the high hall he found a hero standing,
from far lands hailing, him he welcomed.
4.2:
Hloth: “Into high hall now go thou, hero,
and bid Angantýr make answer to me.”

5.1:
“Is Hloth come here, King Heithrek’s heir,
thy bastard brother, thy brother he;
high the young hero his horse doth sit:
would he now, thane, with thee have speech.”

6.1:
Rose outcry in hall; with the atheling stood up,
(the Gothic king, his goodly warriors:)
they all fain would hear what Hloth did say,
and eke what answer Angantýr made.

7.1:
Angantýr: “Hail to thee, Hloth, King Heithrek’s son
and my own brother! On bench sit thou!
In his hall let us drink Heithrek’s arvel
[the father of us, the first of mankind]
in wine or in mead— whiche’er worthiest seemeth.”

8.1:
Hloth: “Not hither came we from Hunnish lands
to share with you your wine and mead—

9.1:
“The half will I have of what Heithrek owned,
of awl and of edge, of all the treasure,
of cow and of call, of quern harsh-grinding,
of thrall and of bond-maid, and those born of them,

10.1:
“the mighty forest which is Murkwood hight,
the hallowed grave which in Gothland stands,
the shining stone which in Danpstead stands,
half of the war-weeds which Heithrek owned,
of lands and lieges and of lustrous arm-rings.”

11.1:
Angantýr: “Your shining shield will be shattered, brother,
and by cold spears will be split many another,
[and many a man will meet his death ]
before Tyrfing in two I sunder,
or to thee, son of Humli, leave the half of it!

12.1:
“Will I give thee, brother, gleaming arm-rings,
much wealth of gold, what most thou wishest—
twelve hundred thralls, twelve hundred steeds,
twelve hundred bond-men with bucklers weaponed.

13.1:
“To every man of you much will I give—
other and better things than ere this he had:
to every man a maid will I give,
and give each maiden a golden necklace.

14.1:
“About thee a-sitting shall I silver heap,
about thee a-going shall I gold-trinkets pour,
so that the rings will roll about thee;
shalt govern a third of Gothic lands.”

15.1:
“Could no better be offered to a bond-woman’s son—
to the son of a bond-woman, though born to a king.
The bastard son then sate on a hill
when the atheling the heirlooms shifted.”

16.1:
Humli: “Shall we feast at our ease till over is winter,
drink and hold converse, quaffing the mead,
and teach our warriors weapons to fashion,
which to battle bravely we shall bear forward.

17.1:
“Well shall we arm the warrior host,
and help thee, Hloth, with hardy deeds;
with twelve-year old draughts, and two-year old foals,
thus shall the host of the Huns be gathered.”

18.1:
Ormar: “Assuredly shall I, with shield aloft,
(to the Hunnish host hurriedly ride,
to summon them to the southern gate)
there ’gainst the Goths to try the game of war.”

19.1:
“From the south am I come, to say these tidings:
burned is the far-famed forest Murkwood,
all Goth-land drenched with the gore of the fallen.

20.1:
“I know that Hervor, Heithrek’s daughter,
and thy sister, by the sword has fallen.
Have Hunnish hosts hewed down the maiden
with many an other of your warriors.

21.1:
.  .  .  .  .  .  .  .
Was she readier for war than with wooer to dally,
or on bench to sit as wedded bride.”

22.1:
“Wast unbrotherly dealt with, my brave sister!
(Now have fallen the fighters who fared with you.)
Full many the men when mead we drank,—
have I fewer followers when I fain would have more.

23.1:
“In all my host no hero see I,
though I should beg him and buy him with rings,
who would raise the war-shield and ride for me
to the Hunnish host to harbinger war.

24.1:
Gizur The Old: “Not a single silverling seek I of thee,
nor of glistening gold guerdon crave I;
yet shall I ride and raise the war-shield,
and to Hunnish hosts herald battle.”
24.2: “To the Huns where shall I herald battle?”

25.1:
Angantýr: “On the down of Dun-heath and in Dylgia-vales
(shall the battle be) ’neath the Iassar-fells’ brow,
where often Goths their glaives reddened,
and victory won warriors in sword-play.”

26.1:
.  .  .  .  .  .  .  .
.  .  .  .  .  .  .  .
“Afraid are your hosts, fey is your leader—
You have angered Óthin: we offer you battle.

27.1:
“On the downs of Dun-heath and in Dylgia-vales
I bid you battle, ’neath the Iassar-fells’ brow.
(May Óthin o’erawe Angantýr’s foes)
and may this spear fly o’er you as I do bid it.”

28.1:
“Seize ye Gizur (the Grýtings’ follower),
Angantýr’s man, from Árheimar come!”

29.1:
Humli: (“No hurt nor harm to him shall be done,
to hero who fares to herald us war.”
29.2:
Gizur: “Will not Hunnish hornbows do harm to us ever,
nor Hunnish wiles hinder our warriors.”)
29.3: “on the downs of Dun-heath and in Dylgia-vales.”

30.1:
“Sixteen squadrons saw I foregathered;
had each squadron fully five thousand men,
and each ‘thousand,’ thirteen hundred,
and each ‘hundred,’ horse-men eight-score.”

31.1:
“Untold arm-rings I offered thee, brother,
a wealth of gold and what most thou didst wish.
As guerdon for strife now hast gotten neither,
nor lands nor lieges nor lustrous rings.

32.1:
“A baleful fate wrought it that, brother, I slew thee!
Will that aye be told. Ill’s the norns’ doom.”

1.1:
Innstein: “Up to Ásmund would all of us
from our dragons hie them,— most doughty men:
In their hall let us burn the host of warriors,
and send to Hel Ásmund’s heroes!”

2.1:
Hálf: “Let half, only, of our host
on our errand to Ásmund fare:
hath he offered us, most open-handed,
many wroughten rings of reddish gold.”

3.1:
Innstein: “You guess not, ring-giver, the guile of Ásmund:
is that crafty king cunning in mind.
If, war-lord, thou our warning heedest,
put little faith in thy stepfather!”

4.1:
Hálf: “Hath Ásmund sworn oaths full many,
and made pledges, as men do know:
will a good liege not give the lie to his oaths,
nor one atheling the other bewray.”

5.1:
Innstein: “Hath Óthin grown angry with thee,
since all too well thou Ásmund trustest:
by wicked wiles he will undo us,
unless on guard against him art!”

6.1:
Hálf: “Aye words of fear art fain to utter:
that prince will not thus break his pledge.
Gold we’ll get there, and goodly things
to have and to hold, from his hoard of rings.”

7.1:
Innstein: “This dream had I— to heed it were wise!—
that flames flickered fiercely about us,
whence hard was it to hack our way.
What deem’st thou, king, this dream betokens?”

8.1:
Hálf: “A guilded helmet shall I give to each
of the fearless heroes that follow me:
would they seem to flash as though fire did blaze
on the hair-hillocks of the hardy men.”

9.1:
Innstein: “Still another dream I after had:
that fire methought to flame on my shoulders;
I guess that little good it bodeth.
What deem’st thou, king, this dream betokens?”

10.1:
Hálf: “Golden byrnies on the backs rattle
of war-workers who in wedges array them:
the shield-bearers’ shoulders they will shine upon,
bright to behold like blazing fire.”

11.1:
Innstein: “A third time still I this did dream:
that in deepest sea we had sunk together;
great tidings this must betoken.
What deem’st thou, king, this dream bodeth?”

12.1:
Hálf: “Be done with dreams and doting talk:
I deem that naught thy dreams betoken.
Say thou no more in my hearing
of these thy dreams from this day onward.”

13.1:
Innstein: “Ye Hrók brothers, in the host of the king,
and Útstein eke: I utter warning!
Let all of us go up to the hall,
and listen not to the liege’s words!”

14.1:
Útstein: “Our brave chieftain shall choose for us,
the foremost in war, how fare we shall:
as the liege liketh so let us, brother,
risk our lives now and the leader follow!”

15.1:
Innstein: “Did our lord listen, in the wars as we lay,
many a time to my counsel;
but now, ween I, he will in naught
give heed to me, since hither we came.”

16.1:
“There’s smoke o’er hawks in the hall of the king:
I wait me the drip of wax from swords.
’Tis time to deal out treasure and gold
among Hálf’s heroes, and helmets eke.

17.1:
“That would I now that Hálf awake:
are fires kindled unquenchable.
To Ásmund oughtest, wise atheling,
to the grim-minded, his gifts requite!

18.1:
“Let us bravely batter the beer-hall’s walls!
Gape even now the gable walls;
will ever be sung, while earth lasteth,
how Hálf’s heroes hardily fared.

19.1:
“Briskly forward, nor back a foot!
Will the war-workers have to wield their swords:
will themselves be seared with sore gashes
and sore wounds, ere the battle is stilled.

20.1:
“Let the warriors wend their way quickly
out of the fire with the atheling!
Forever liveth not any man:
will the folk-warder not fear to die.”

21.1:
“Here saw I all, equally bold,
fearlessly follow the folk-warder:
well met, again, when after we meet!
Than death, life is not lighter to bear!”

22.1:
“Is Hrok fallen with Hálf the king—
the fearless one at the feet of his lord;
but ill owe we to Óthin now
who overthrew a thane so brave.

23.1:
“Eighteen summers I did follow
the ruler, roving, to redden spears;
no other king eager for war
shall I ever have, to grow old with him.

24.1:
“Will Innstein here to the earth sink dead,
whole-hearted henchman, by the head of his king.
will men e’er after to mind call it
that laughing died this lord of men.”

1.1:
(“ ’Tis time to tell, on turf as I lie,
felled by the sword, what fate was ours:
unlike our lot in life hath been,
to Hel fare I while whole thou livest.)
1.2:
“I little bethought me of laws like these—
that me, single-handed, many would challenge
when as their champion the Huns chose me,
eight times over, for the atheling’s realm.

2.1:
“Not easy is it ever to know
who will be born his brother’s slayer.
Did Drótt bear thee in Danish lands;
myself she bore in Sweden’s realm.
2.2:
“I grappled with one, and again with two—
with four and five of their followers;
with six and seven at the same time, then,
and one against eight: a wonder I live!

3.2:
“But then wavered, wincing, my courage
when eleven warriors me alone bestead,
ere that in my sleep said to me wraiths
that I should dare to do battle.

4.1:
“Trusty broad-swords twain were forged—
heirlooms from Buthli; now one is broken.
So deftly had the dwarfs forged them
as none e’er did or will do, hereafter.
4.2:
“Then came the hoary Hildibrand,
the Hunnish warrior; nor he my match:
I marked on him, his helmet beneath,
a deadly wound, dealt with the sword.”

5.1:
“By my head, broken, my buckler stands,
(round-shaped, shining, but shattered now;)
on it are scored eighty notches
for doughty men given to death by me.

6.1:
“My liefest son lies by my head,
the after-heir whom I did have—
.  .  .  .  .  .  .  .
unwittingly in war I slew him.

7.1:
“One boon, brother, I beg of thee—
one boon only albeit one
which slayer not often to slain man grants:
in thy weeds of war wind my body!

8.1:
“(Have hateful norns knit our fate-thread:
to fight against fate the fey one avails not:)
lifeless shall I now lie on the ground,
slain by the sword, sorely wounded.”

1.1:
Hearken, ye ring-bearers, while of Harold I tell you,
the mightily wealthy, and his manful war-deeds;
words I o’erheard a maiden high-minded speaking,
golden-haired, white-armed, with a glossy-beaked raven.

2.1:
Wise thought her the valkyrie; were welcome never
men to the bright-eyed one, her who birds’ speech knew well.
Greeted the light-lashed maiden, the lily-throated woman,
the Hymir’s-skull-cleaver as on cliff he was perching.

3.1:
“How is it, ye ravens— whence are ye come now
with beaks all gory, at break of morning?
Carrion-reek ye carry, and your claws are bloody.
Were ye near, at night-time, where ye knew of corpses?”

4.1:
Shook himself the dun-hued one, and dried his beak,
the eagle’s oath-brother, and of answer bethought him:
“Harold we follow, Halfdan’s first-born,
I the young Yngling, since out of egg we crept.

5.1:
“That king thou knowest, him who at Kvinnar dwelleth,
the hoard-warder of North men, who has hollow war-ships
with reddish ribs and with reddened war-shields,
with tarred oar-blades and with tents foam-besprinkled.

6.1:
“Fain outside would he drink the ale at Yule-tide,
the fight-loving folk-warder, and Frey’s-game play there.
Even half-grown, he hated the hearthfire cozy,
the warm women’s room, and the wadded down-mittens.

7.1:
“Hearken how the high-born one in the Hafrs-firth fought there,
the keen-eyed king’s son, against Kiotvi the wealthy:
came the fleet from the eastward, eager for fighting,
with gaping figureheads and graven ship-prows.

8.1:
“They were laden with franklins and lindenshields gleaming,
with Westland spearshafts and with Welsh broadswords.
The berserkers bellowed as the battle opened,
the wolf-coats shrieked loud and shook their weapons.

9.1:
“Their strength would they try, but he taught them to flee,
the lord of the Eastmen who at Útstein dwelleth.
The steeds-of-Nokkvi he steered out when started the battle.
Then boomed the bucklers ere a blow felled Haklang.

10.1:
“The thick-necked atheling behind the isle took shelter:
he grew loath, against Lúfa to hold the land of his fathers.
Then hid under benches, and let their buttocks stick up,
they who were wounded, but thrust their heads keelward.

11.1:
“Their shoulders shielded the shifty heroes—
were they showered with slung-shot— with the shingles-of-Gladhome.
Home from Hafrs-firth hastened they eastward,
fled by way of Iathar, of ale-cups thinking.

12.1:
“On the gravel lay the fallen, given to the one-eyed
husband of Fulla; were we fain of such doings.

13.1:
“Of more and other things shall the maids of Ragnhild,
the haughty women-folk, now have to gabble
than of the heath-dwellers which Harold not ever
feasted on the fallen, as their friends had done oft.

14.1:
“The high-born liege-lord took the lady from Denmark—
broke with his Rogaland sweethearts and their sisters from Horthaland,
with those from Heithmork and Hálogaland eke.”

15.1:
The Valkyrie: “Whether is open-handed he-who-hastens-the-battle,
to those who fend faithfully foemen from his homeland?”

16.1:
The Raven: “With much goods are gladdened the gallant warriors,
who in the hall of Harold while the time with chess-play:
with much wealth he rewards them, and with well-forged broadswords,
with gold from Hunland and with girls from the Eastfolks.

17.1:
“Most happy are they when there is hope for battle,
all ready to rouse them and to row strongly,
so as to snap the thongs and to sunder the thole-pins,
to churn the brine briskly at the beck of their liege-lord.”

18.1:
The Valkyrie: “Of the skalds’ lot would I ask thee, since thou skill of that boastest:
how the bards fare there thou full well knowest—
    they who are in Harold’s hall.”

19.1:
The Raven: “Is seen from their raiment and their red-gold finger-rings
    that a kind king they have.
Red fur-cloaks own they, most fairly bordered,
swords wound with silver, and sarks ring-woven,
gilded baldricks and graven helmets,
heavy gold bracelets which Harold bestowed on them.”

20.1:
The Valkyrie: “Of the berserkers’ lot would I ask thee, thou who batten’st on corpses:
how fare the fighters who rush forth to battle,
    and stout-hearted stand ’gainst the foe?”

21.1:
The Raven: “Wolf-coats are they called, the warriors unfleeing,
    who bear bloody shields in battle;
the darts redden where they dash into battle
    and shoulder to shoulder stand.
’T is men tried and true only, who can targes shatter,
whom the wise war-lord wants in battle.”

22.1:
The Valkyrie: “Of Andath and all his ilk, too, have I asked thee but little:
how fare the fiddlers, how fare the jugglers
    in the halls of Harold?”

2.1:
“Lords from man-home are to be looked for,
high-born and hardy, which my heart gladdens.

3.1:
“What thunders, Bragi, as though thousands stirred,
    or whelming hosts?”
3.2:
Bragi: “Crack all boards of the benches as though Baldr were coming
    back to Óthin’s beer-hall.”

4.1:
Óthin: “Of witless words shalt beware, wise Bragi,
    for full well thou wotst:
’t is Eric this heralds, who to us is wending,
    the earl, into Óthin’s hall.

5.1:
“Sigmund and Sinfiotli, leave your seats, ye heroes,
    and go forth to greet the king!
Bid him enter in, if Eric it be:
    him I have hopes to see.”

6.1: Sigmund: “Why of Eric, rather than of another?”
6.2:
Óthin: “Because in many a liege-land this lord hath warred
    and borne a bloody sword.”

7.1: Sigmund: “Why, then, didst rob him of victory, since valiant thou thought’st him?”
7.2:
Óthin:     “No one knoweth—
looks the grey wolf (grimly) toward the gods’ dwellings.”

8.1:
Sigmund: “Hail to thee, Eric, here thou art welcome!
    wise war-lord, in hall.
This fain would I know: who be following thee
    of athelings, from the edge-fight?”

9.1:
Eric: “Kings five there are, them all I shall name thee:
    am I the sixth myself.”

1.1:
Gautatýr sent forth Gondul and Skogul
    to choose among kings’ kinsmen:
who of Yngvi’s offspring should with Óthin dwell,
    and wend with him to Valholl.

2.1:
They found Biorn’s brother his byrnie donning,
under standard standing the stalwart leader—
were darts uplifted and spearshafts lowered;
    up the strife then started.

3.1:
Called on Hálogaland’s heroes and Horthaland’s swordsmen
the Northmen’s folkwarder, ere he fared to battle:
a good host had he of henchmen from Norway—
the Danes’-terror donned his bronze-helm.

4.1:
Threw down his war-weeds, thrust off his byrnie
the great-hearted lord, ere began the battle—
laughed with his liege-men; his land would he shield now,
the gladsome hero ’neath gold-helm standing.

5.1:
Cut then keenly the king’s broadsword
through foemen’s war-weeds, as though water it sundered.
Clashed then spear-blades, cleft were war-shields;
did ring-decked war-swords rattle on helmets.

6.1:
Were targes trodden by the Týr-of-shields,
by the hard-footed hilt-blade, and heads eke of Northmen;
battle raged on the island, athelings reddened
the shining shield-castles with shedded life-blood,

7.1:
Burned the wound-fires in bloody gashes,
were the long-beards lifted against the life of warriors—
the sea-of-wounds surged high around the swords’ edges,
ran the stream-of-arrows on the strand of Storth-isle.

8.1:
Reddened war-shields rang ’gainst each other,
did Skogul’s-stormblasts scar red targes;
billowed blood-waves in the blast-of-Óthin—
was many a man’s son mowed down in battle.

9.1:
Sate then the liege-lords with swords brandished,
with shields shattered and shredded byrnies:
not happy in their hearts was that host of men,
    and to Valholl wended their way.

10.1:
Spoke then Gondul, on spearshaft leaning:
    “groweth now the gods’ following,
since Hákon hath been with host so goodly
    hidden home by holy gods.”

11.1:
Heard the war-lord what the valkyries spoke of,
    high-hearted, on horsehack—
wisely they bore them, sitting war-helmeted,
    and with shields them sheltering.

12.1:
“Why didst Geirskogul, grudge us victory?
Yet worthy were we that the gods granted it.”

13.1:
“ ’Tis owing to us that the issue was won
    and your foemen did flee.

14.1:
Ride forth now shall we,” said fierce Skogul,
    “to the green homes of the godheads,—
there to tell Óthin that the atheling will now
    come to see him himself.”

16.1:
Said the war-worker, wending from battle—
    was his byrnie all bloody:
“Angry-minded Óthin meseemeth.
    Be we heedful of his hate!”

17.1:
“All einheriar shall swear oaths to thee:
    share thou the æsir’s ale,
thou enemy-of-earls! Here within hast thou
    brethren eight,” said Bragi.

18.1:
“Our gear of war,” said the goodly king,
    “we mean to keep in our might.
helmet and hauberk one should heed right well:
    ’tis good to guard one’s spear.”

19.1:
Then was it seen how that sea-king had
    upheld the holy altars,
since Hákon all did hail with welcome,
    both gods and heavenly hosts.

20.1:
On a good day is born that great-souled lord
    who hath a heart like his;
aye will his times be told of on earth,
    and men will speak of his might.

21.1:
Unfettered will fare the Fenriswolf,
    and fall on the fields of men,
ere that there cometh a kingly lord
    as good, to stand in his stead.

22.1:
Cattle die and kinsmen die,
    land and lieges are whelmed;
since Hákon to the heathen gods fared
    many a host is harried.

1.1:
Widely is flung, warning of slaughter,
the weaver’s-beam’s-web: ’t is wet with blood;
is spread now, grey, the spear-thing before,
the woof-of-the-warriors which valkyries fill
with the red-warp-of- Randvér’s-banesman.

2.1:
Is this web woven and wound of entrails,
and heavy weighted with heads of slain;
are blood-bespattered spears the treadles,
iron-bound the beams, the battens, arrows:
let us weave with our swords this web of victory!

3.1:
Goes Hild to weave, and Hiorthrimul,
Sangrith and Svipul, with swords brandished:
shields will be shattered, shafts will be splintered,
will the hound-of-helmets the hauberks bite.

4.1:
Wind we, wind we the-web-of-darts,
and follow the atheling after to war!
Will men behold shields hewn and bloody
where Gunn and Gondul have guarded the thane.

5.1:
Wind we, wind we such web-of-darts
as the young war-worker waged afore-time!
Forth shall we fare where the fray is thickest,
where friends and fellows ’gainst foemen battle!

6.1:
Wind we, wind we the web-of-darts
where float the flags of unflinching men!
Let not the liege’s life be taken:
valkyries award the weird of battle.

7.1:
Will seafaring men hold sway over lands,
who erstwhile dwelled on outer nesses;
is doomed to die a doughty king,
lies slain an earl by swords e’en now

8.1:
Will Irish men eke much ill abide:
’t will not ever after be out of men’s minds.
Now the web is woven, and weapons reddened—
in all lands will be heard the heroes’ fall.

9.1:
Now awful is it to be without,
as blood-red rack races overhead;
is the welkin gory with warriors’ blood
as we valkyries war-songs chanted.

10.1:
Well have we chanted charms full many
about the king’s son: may it bode him well!
Let him learn them who listens to us,
and speak these spells to spearmen after.

11.1:
Start we swiftly with steeds unsaddled—
hence to battle with brandished swords!

1.1:
“Here liest thou, Hring, Lord of the Gauts,
the most headstrong of human kind—
minded, to-morrow to murther thy son:
will this foul deed be told far and wide.

2.1:
“Hear thou Busla’s song— ’t will be sung full soon;
so that it be heard the whole world about—
harmful to him who heareth it,
but fellest for him whom fain I would curse.

3.1:
“May wights be wildered, and wonders happen,
may cliffs be shattered and the world shaken,
may the weather worsen, and wonders happen,
but thou, King Hring, forgive Herrauth,
 and eke to Bósi no ill threaten.

4.1:
“O’er thy chest such charms now chant I shall
that evil asps shall eat thy heart,
that thy ears henceforth shall hear no more,
and thy seeing eyes leave their sockets,
 but thou with Bósi wilt bear, hereafter,
 nor harbor hate against Herrauth, either.

5.1:
“If boat thou sailest, shall burst the ropes,
if boat thou steerest, shall break the tholepins—
shall the sail-cloth be slit and sag downward,
and all the tackle be torn asunder,
 but thou harbor no hate against Herrauth,
 and but thou with Bósi will bear hereafter.

6.1:
“Shall the reins ravel when thou ridest forth,
shall horses go halt, and nags be hamstrung—
shall both highways and bridle-paths
take thee where trolls may tear thee straightway,
 but thou with Bósi wilt bear hereafter,
 nor harbor hate against Herrauth, either.

7.1:
“May thy bed be for thee like burning straw,
thy high-seat unsteady like heaving sea-wave.
Yet woe awaits thee much worse by far:
if with maid thou meanest a man’s joy to have,
shalt lose thy way then: doest wish to hear more?”

8.1:
“Shall trolls and elves and tricking witches,
shall dwarfs and etins burn down thy mead-hall—
shall thurses hate thee and horses ride thee,
shall all straws stick thee, all storms stun thee:
and woe worth thee but my will thou doest!”

9.1:
Come here six fellows: say thou their names:
I shall show them to thee unshackled all.
But thou get them guessed as good meseemeth,
shall ravening hounds rive thee to pieces,
and thy soul sink to hell-fire!”

1.1:
Gestumblindi: “That would I have which I had yesterday;
    heed what I had:
men’s hamperer, word’s hinderer,
    and speeder of speech.
Aright read now this riddle, Heithrek!”
1.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
give him ale! That hampers many a man’s wits; by it, some become talkative, but other men’s wits are mazed.”

2.1:
Gestumblindi: “From home I hied me, and from home faring
    I saw a way of ways:
was a way beneath and a way above,
    and ways there were on all sides.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
2.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
You went over a bridge, the river ran under it, the birds flew above your head and on either side of you—that was their way.”

3.1:
Gestumblindi: “What drink was it I drank yesterday?
    ’twas neither wine nor water,
neither mead nor ale, nor meat, either;
    yet went I thirstless thence.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
3.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is.
you lay down in the shade where the dew had fallen on the grass, and this cooled your lips and quenched your thirst.

4.1:
Gestumblindi: “Harshly he clangs, on hard paths treading
    which he has fared before.
Two mouths he has, and mightily kisses,
    and on gold alone he goes.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
4.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is the goldsmith’s hammer with which gold is beaten.”

5.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who is the great one that glides o’er the earth,
    and swallows both waters and woods?
The wind he fears, but wights nowise,
    and seeks to harm the sun.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
5.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
That is the fog. One cannot see the sun because of him, but he disappears when the wind blows, and men can do naught against him. He kills the light of the sun.”

6.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who is the mighty one who o’er much has sway,
    the half of whom turns toward Hel?
He saves many men but slashes the earth,
    if fast with trusty friend.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
6.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
That is the anchor, with a stout and strong rope. It guards many a ship. It grips the earth with one fluke which thus turns Hel-ward. Many a man has been saved by it.”

7.1:
Gestumblindi: “On high fells what lives? What falls in deep dales?
Without air what lives? What is not ever silent?
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
7.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
the raven always lives on high fells, the dew always falls in
deep dales, the fish live without air, and the roaring waterfall is never silent.”

8.1:
Gestumblindi: “What marvel is it which without I saw,
    before Delling’s-door,
with his head ever Hel-ward turning,
    with his feet seeking the sun.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
8.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
That is the leek: its head turns into the earth, but the leaves, upward.”

9.1:
Gestumblindi: “What marvel is it which without I saw,
    before Delling’s-door?
Were twain briskly, and breathless withal.
    boiling a wand-of-wounds.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
9.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
they are the smith’s bellows; they blow but have no breath.”

10.1:
Gestumblindi: “What marvel is it which without I saw,
    before Delling’s-door?
The white fliers on the flagstones bounded.
    but the swart ones sank in the sand.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
10.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
they are hail and rain; because the hail beats on the flags, but the rain drops sink in the sand and go into the ground.”

11.1:
Gestumblindi: “What marvel is it which without I saw,
    before Delling’s-door?
A black boar saw I bask in the mud,
    yet no bristles stood on his back.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
11.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is the dung-beetle.”

12.1:
Gestumblindi: “What marvel is it which without I saw,
    before Delling’s-door?
Ten tongues has it, has twenty eyes
and forty feet, slowly fares that wight.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
12.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
you saw a sow in the farmyard with nine shoats in her.” Then the king had the sow killed, and nine pigs were found in her, just as Gestumblindi had said.

13.1:
Gestumblindi: “What marvel is it which without I saw,
    before Delling’s-door?
Upward it flies with eagle’s voice,
    and hard grip its claws the helmet.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
13.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is the arrow.”

14.1:
Gestumblindi: “What marvel is it which without I saw,
    before Delling’s-door?
Eight feet it has and four eyes,
    and its knees are above its belly.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
14.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
it is the spider.”

15.1:
Gestumblindi: “What marvel is it which without I saw,
    before Delling’s-door?
It lights for men, and swallows up lights,
    and wolves seek ever to win it.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
15.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is the Sun. He lights all the world and shines on all men; but there are two wolves, hight Skalli and Hatti, one of whom goes before, and the other follows, the sun.”

16.1:
Gestumblindi: “What marvel is it which without I saw,
    before Delling’s-door?
Harder than horn, blacker than Hel,
whiter than shell of egg, straighter than shaft of spear.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
16.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is obsidian, with the sun shining on it.”

17.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
you saw two female swans going to their nests to lay their eggs. Their shells are neither hand-made nor wrought by hammers; but the he-swan sits out on the islands, he that gat their eggs with them.”

18.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who be the women on wilding fell?
    One bears a babe by the other,
and maid by maid a man-child begets,
    yet man has not touched these maids.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
18.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
they are two angelica stalks standing together, with a shoot coming up between them.”

19.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who be the women who, weaponless,
    for their king kill each other?
Every day the dark ones shield him,
    but the fair ones aye go forth.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
19.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
That is the game of hneftafl: weaponless, the figures slay each other for the sake of their king. The red ones are his followers.

20.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who be the playmates that pass over the lands,
    seeming fair to their father?
A white shield they show in winter,
    and a swart one in summer.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
20.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
they are the ptarmigans. They are white in winter and black in summer.”

21.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who be the sisters that sorrowing fare,
    seeming fair to their father?
Many a man their might hath known—
    and thus they live their lives.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
21.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
They are the billows. They are called the maids of Ægir.”

22.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who be the maids that fare, many together,
    seeming fair to their father?
Whitish hair have the white-hooded ones,
    and no man is with the maids.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
22.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
but these are the waves, as before.”

23.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who be the widows that band all together,
    seeming fair to their father?
They are seldom kind to sailor-folk,
    and are wide awake in the wind.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
23.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
they are Ægir’s widows. Thus are called the breakers.”

24.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who be the women that wade in the surf
    and fare along the firths?
A hard bed have the white-hooded ones,
    and quiet are they in calm.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
24.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
they are the billows—their beds are skerries and shingle, and they become somewhat sluggish in calm weather.”

25.1:
Gestumblindi: “I saw traveling a soil’s-earth-dweller,
    a corpse sate on a corpse;
one blind rode a blind thing to the billows’-road,
    and no life was in the nag.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
25.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
you came to a river, and an ice-floe floated down it. On the floe lay a dead horse, and on the horse, a dead snake; so that one blind thing rode another blind thing.”

26.1:
Gestumblindi: “What creature kills the cattle men have,
    and is iron-clad, without?
Eight horns it has, but head it has none,
    and runs when run it may.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
26.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is the húnn on the checkerboard. It shares its name with the bear, and it runs as soon as it is overthrown.”

27.1:
Gestumblindi: “What beast is it which brave men shelters?
It has a bloody back and wards off blows,
goes against spears, life-giving to some.
Against lords’ left hand it lays its body.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
27.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is the shield. It often becomes bloody in battle, shielding those men who are handy with it.”

28.1:
Gestumblindi: “Greatly had grown a goose with big neb,
had brought timber together, for goslings eager.
Gave shelter to her the sheaves’-bite-swords;
but above it lay the drink’s- dinful-rockcave,
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
28.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is a duck which had built her nest between the jaws of an ox, with the skull roofing above it.”

29.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is a cow. She has four feet and four tits, two horns and two eyes, and her tail drags after her.”

30.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who is the one that in the ashpit sleeps:
    and is only struck out of stone?
Neither father nor mother has the greedy fiend—
    there he wants to live his life.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
30.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is the fire hidden in the hearth—it is struck out of flint.”

31.1:
Gestumblindi: “A stallion stood bestriding a mare;
he put buttock ’neath belly and bobbed with his tail.
Draw it out and in, work at it long!
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
31.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that horse is a piece of linen on the loom. His mare is the weaver’s reed, and up and down is the web to be shaken.”

32.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who be the thanes to the thing who ride?
    Sixteen are in that set.
Their liege-men send they over all the lands,
    to seek a place to settle.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
32.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
they are Itrek and Andath sitting on their checkerboard.”

33.1:
Gestumblindi: “In the summer saw I, at sunset time,
a merry band at festive board;
the men did drink their mead in peace,
the while the mead-keg muttering stood.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
33.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is a sow with her shoats. When the pigs suck her she grunts, while they keep quiet.”

34.1:
Gestumblindi: “Maidens saw I which were much like dust;
    boulders served them as beds.
Are they swart and sallow in sunny weather,
    but the fairer, the fainter the light.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
34.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
they are the gledes dying on the hearth.”

35.1:
Gestumblindi: “On a sail I sate and saw dead men
who a blood-vein bore to the bark of a tree.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
35.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
You sate on a wall and saw a falcon bear an eider duck to the cliff.”

36.1:
Gestumblindi: “Who are the twain that on ten feet run?
three eyes they have, but only one tail.
Aright guess now this riddle, Heithrek!”
36.2:
Heithrek: “Good is thy riddle, Gestumblindi,
    and guessed it is:
that is Óthin riding on Sleipnir.”

37.1:
Gestumblindi: “Guess one more riddle, since wiser thou seemest
    than any other wight:
what said Óthin in Baldr’s ear
    before he was borne to the fire?”
37.2:
Heithrek: “But wicked spells and wantonness
    I ween that it was:
the words thou spakest no wight knoweth
    but thou, ill and unclean wight.”

1.1:
Of life and goods did the grim warrior
    rob men wrongfully;
by the way which was watched by him,
    no quick wight ever came.

2.1:
By himself (most often) he ate alone,
    nor e’er bade men to his meals;
till once, weary and weak of strength
    a wayfarer he welcomed.

3.1:
Of meat and drink he seemed much in need,
    and faint without food;
now, frightened, he must fain trust him
    who ere had been hard of heart.

4.1:
Gave he meat and drink to the drooping man,
    and whole-heartedly, withal;
good fare he gave him, of God mindful,
    for well he wished the man.

5.1:
Up he got, on ill deeds bent,
    nor gratefully took what was given:
his sin swelled, he the sleeping man murdered
    who wise and wary was else.

6.1:
To Heavens’ God for help he prayed
    when waking, wounded to death;
but on him fell the heavy sin:
    who had dastardly done him to death.

7.1:
Came holy angels from Heaven above,
    and swiftly seized his soul;
A sinless life will it lead thereafter,
    aye with almighty God.

8.1:
Nor health nor wealth— though all go well with him—
    may a man ever master;
misfortune befalls him who feared it least:
    by himself, no one settles the issue.

9.1:
Neither Unnar nor Sævaldi would e’er have thought
    that fortune would fail them at last;
naked they both were banished from men,
    and ran as “wolves” to the woods.

10.1:
The might of love hath brought many to grief:
    oft cometh woe of women:
they grew evil though God almighty
    had created them clean.

11.1:
Sworn friends they were, Sváfath and Skart-hethin,
    nor would one be without the other;
till by one woman bewitched they were:
    was she born to undo them both.

12.1:
Listless of all, for love of the girl—
    of games and gatherings—
no other thing could they think about,
    for love of the lily-white maid.

13.1:
Were dreary for them the darksome nights,
    nor could they slumber or sleep;
till out of that grief there grew up hate
    ’twixt men who were friends before.

14.1:
Of monstrous things, as is mostly the case,
    the outcome was seen full soon:
on the holm they went for the winsome maid,
    and did each other to death.

15.1:
let man beware of o’erweening pride—
    that have I seen in sooth;
for away from God they wander all
    who keep them not clean of it.

16.1:
Were mighty and rich Ráthný and Vébothi,
    and deemed they did but good;
now near the fire they nurse their wounds,
    warming now one now the other.

17.1:
Their strength they trusted, and strove to be
    more mighty than all the others;
their deserts, however, seemed to God
    to merit a different mead.

18.1:
A life of lust they lived, many-wise,
    and of gold and jewels had joy:
their reward now have they as walk they must
    between the frost and the fire.

19.1:
In sworn foes put thy faith never,
    though they woo thee with winsome words;
speak fair to them, but others’ fate
    ’tis well to take as a warning.

20.1:
Found it Sorli so, the simple-hearted,
    when he left the award to Vígolf;
he blindly trusted his brother’s banesman,
    who soon betrayed his trust.

22.1:
On the following day befell it then:
    when riding to Rýgiar-dale,
they did to death who had done them naught,
    and left his body lifeless,

23.1:
his hacked corse hauled by hidden path,
    and dropped it down a well:
from the light would hide it; but the Lord did see,
    the holy one, from his heaven.

24.1:
The true God then bade the good one’s soul
    to enter into his bliss;
but his evil foes will not early be
    relieved from e’erlasting pain.

25.1:
Pray the “disar,” the dear Lord’s friends,
    be gracious and grant thee their favor:
a week after will everything
    go as well as thou couldst wish.

26.1:
What rashly thou wrought’st in anger—
    do not add more ill to it,
but with good deeds soothe who was grieved by you;
    that, say they, is good for the soul.

27.1:
To God shalt ever for good things pray,—
    to him who hath made all men;
woefully ill fares every one
    who does not find his father.

28.1:
Above all, beg that boon of him
    of which thou know’st most need;
he misses all who asks for naught:
    heeds no one the silent one’s needs.

29.1:
Tardily came I, though called early,
    to the threshold of the throne.
Thither will I, for that was the pledge:
    gets the prize who pleadeth most.

30.1:
Our sins cause it that with sorrow we fare
    out of this world of woe;
need no one dread who did no ill:
    ’t is well to be without blemish.

31.1:
Like unto wolves I ween they be
    who have a fickle heart;
will they find it thus whose feet will have
    to fare on fiery paths.

32.1:
Friendly redes shrewd, tied in a sheaf,
    sage counsels seven I teach thee;
heed thou give them, nor forget them ever:
    in good stead will they stand thee.

33.1:
It behooves me tell how happy I was
    and prized this world of pleasure;
and this also, how the sons of men
    dread to die from this world.

34.1:
Pride and lust overpower those men
    who wish for worldly goods:
the shining gold brings grief e’erlasting—
    hath wealth mocked full many.

35.1:
Aye fond of much men found me here,
    for little had I learned:
this life below the Lord hath made
    full of lust and feasting.

36.1:
Full long I sate, in sickness drooping—
    much then me listed to live;
but he prevailed who had more power:
    was I doomed to suffer death.

38.1:
I alone knew in all ways how
    sorrows were heaped on my head:
a world of horror those maids of hell
    did show me every eve.

39.1:
The sun I saw, the day-star in sooth,
    droop in the world of din;
but Hel’s gate heard I on the other hand
    grate with grinding.

40.1:
The sun I saw, setting blood-red,
    when ready to wend from this world;
mighty he seemed in many ways—
    far more than before.

41.1:
The sun I saw: it seemed to me
    as on God Almighty I gazed;
lowly before him the last time I bowed,
    in this world of living wights.

42.1:
The sun I saw, and so he shone
    that bereft of my senses I seemed;
but over against him Gylfi’s stream roared
    in its bed, all mixed with blood.

43.1:
The sun I saw with trembling sight,
    affrighted and faint I was;
for most woefully was my heart
    rent and torn in twain.

45.1:
The sun I saw, and since never,
    after that dreary day;
far away the waters vanished:
    cold, I parted from care.

46.1:
From my breast did fly,— then born I was—
    and hence, my star of hope:
high it hovered, hastening on,
    never ceased it to soar.

47.1:
Longer than any lasted that night
    when, stiff, I lay on the straw;
which soothly shows, as saith our Lord,
    that man is made of the mould.

48.1:
Knoweth, alas! the loving God,
    He who made heaven and earth,
unloved how many must leave this world,
    though kith and kin they had.

49.1:
Of his works, every one the reward reapeth:
    happy he who does good:
away from wealth, was I given
    a grave, dug in the gravel.

50.1:
The lust of the flesh oft lures on men—
    have many too much of that;
the water of cleansing was to me
    aye the most hateful of all.

52.1:
Meseemed, through seven seats of victory
    I fared, without and within;
below and above I sought better ways,
    where most easily I could fare.

53.1:
Now sooth I say of what first I saw
    as I passed to the world of pain:
with singed wings, birds— souls they were—
    flew there as many as midges.

54.1:
From the West saw I the Water-dragon fly—
    he lighted on Lucifer’s path;
his wings he shook so that far and wide
    were heaved up heaven and hell.

55.1:
The Sun-stag saw I, from the South faring—
    he tethered the two together;
with his feet standing steadfast on earth,
    his horns touching very heaven.

56.1:
From the North there came kinsmen riding—
    seven saw I of them:
out of full beakers pure beer they quaffed
    from out of Baugregin’s burn.

57.1:
The wind ceased, the water stopped;
    then heard I dreadful din:
unfaithful wives for their wicked lovers
    ground there mould for meat.

58.1:
The dark women in dreary wise
    ground with the gory stones;
their bloody hearts, heavy with sorrow,
    about their breasts did hang.

59.1:
Many a man maimed I saw,
    walking the glowing ways.
Methought their faces befouled all were
    with the gore of women beguiled.

60.1:
Many a man to mould had grown
    who sacred supper ne had;
did heathen stars stand above them,
    blazing with baleful runes.

61.1:
Men saw I there who much did feel
    envy of other men’s lot:
about their breasts were bloody runes
    marked with evil malice.

62.1:
Men saw I there, many, cheerless,
    faring wilding ways:
is rewarded thus in this world who
    fell a prey to follies.

63.1:
Men saw I there who in many ways
    had stolen what others owned;
in flocks they fared to Fégiarn’s castle,
    laden with burdens of lead.

64.1:
Men saw I then who many a one
    had robbed of riches and life;
poison-fanged snakes pierced these knaves,
    thrusting through their breasts.

65.1:
Men saw I then unmindful, in life,
    to hold dear the holy days:
were their hands now nailed on hot stones,
    as painful punishment.

66.1:
Men saw I then of mighty pride,
    who held their heads too high:
were their weeds all wondrously
    lined with living fire.

67.1:
Men saw I then who many times
    had falsely lied on their fellows.
Now Hell’s ravens hacked felly
    their eyes out of their heads.

68.1:
Thou canst not ever know all the pangs
    which the damned have in hell;
their sweet sins turn to sore anguish:
    is pleasure e’er followed by pain.

69.1:
Men saw I then, with merciful heart
    who had helped the humble;
heavenly angels sang hymns above,
    and read holy books, over their heads.

70.1:
Men saw I then who had mortified
    with much fasting their flesh:
the angels of God bowed to all of them,
    which is highest bliss in heaven.

71.1:
Men saw I then who had meted out
    meat for the weary ones’ mouths:
was their resting place on rays of heaven,
    forever at ease and in bliss.

72.1:
Had holy maidens wholly cleansed and
    washed the souls of sin,
of those men who on many days
    had scourged and scathed themselves.

73.1:
Men saw I then in much who had
    heeded the laws of the Lord;
were clean candles kindled over them
    which shone, burning brightly.

74.1:
Saw I high wains fare the heavens along—
    their ways led to the Lord;
those men steered them who were murdered,
    though sinless themselves.

75.1:
Oh mighty Father, oh matchless Son,
    oh Holy Ghost of Heaven:
hearken to our prayer who hast made us,
    to free us all from evil!

76.1:
Hringvor and Listvor sit at Herthi’s door,
    singing their siren strains:
the Norn’s blood from their noses drips,
    which whetteth hate among men.

77.1:
Óthin’s wife on earth’s ship rows,
    lusting after love;
’twill be late, ere that she lowers her sails,
    which are fastened by fleshly lusts.

78.1:
Of thy heirloom, father, had I the care—
    I and Sólkatla’s sons;
of the horn of that hart out of howe which bore
    wise Vígdvalin.

79.1:
Here are runes which written have
    the nine daughters of Niorth:
Baugveig the eldest, Kreppvor the youngest,
    and their seven sisters.

80.1:
Every mortal sin committed they,
    Sváfr and Sváfrlogi;
made well out the blood and sucked the wounds—
    ever ill in their ways.

81.1:
The lay which now learned thou hast
    thou shalt speak and spread ’mongst the quick:
the Sun Song, which in sooth will be
    found to be lying least.

82.1:
Now must we part, but shall meet again
    when we rise again in gladness;
may our dear Lord grant their rest to the dead,
    and eke his love to the living.
